 With 60 new cases in the past week, Florida’s dengue total jumps to 485
 News brief 
 Stephanie Soucheray, MA 
 Topics 
 Dengue 
 Share 
 Copied to clipboard 
 Andrei Sauko / iStock 
 Florida’s Department of Health recorded 60 more locally acquired dengue cases in the past week, bringing the state total to 485 . This is the highest case count in decades, and significantly higher than last year’s total, which was 62 cases.   
 Of the 485 cases, 385 confirmed cases come from Hillsborough County, where a local emergency has been extended through this week. Eleven other counties in the state have also reported infections, and 20 mosquito pools have been reported.   
 “Mosquito Management crews are increasing treatments by air and ground because the County's mosquito surveillance in many neighborhoods is showing dengue virus activity in the mosquito population,” the county said in a press release on the emergency.   
 Dengue, also called breakbone fever, is spread by Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes. Most people infected will recover, but can report high fevers, severe muscular and joint pain, and headaches. The virus can also be deadly. Last month, a Tampa-area woman because the state’s first dengue death in decades.   
 Quick takes: Salmonella tied to oysters, Bundibugyo vaccine funding, no mother-to-child HIV in Barbados
 News brief 
 Chris Dall, MA 
 Topics 
 Ebola 
 HIV/AIDS 
 Salmonella 
 The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is reporting one new Salmonella case in a multistate outbreak linked to raw oysters. There have now been 28 cases in 13 states, with five people hospitalized. The outbreak of Salmonella Telelkebir is linked to oysters harvested from the Little Wicomico River harvest area in Virginia from September 18 to October 8 by the Little Wicomico Oyster Company, according to the Food and Drug Administration . The company has recalled the oysters, and consumers, restaurants, and food retailers who bought the oysters are advised to dispose of them and sanitize any containers or surfaces they touched.
 The International AIDS Vaccine Initiative (IAVI) announced last week that it has been awarded $36 million by the Administration for Strategic Preparedness and Response’s Biomedical Advanced Research and Development Authority (BARDA) to advance development of its one-dose vaccine against Bundibugyo Ebola virus. The award will support manufacturing of vaccine doses for clinical evaluation and outbreak response, along with options for expanded manufacturing to support future preparedness needs. The rVSV-based vaccine platform is one of four being evaluated for Bundibugyo, which is the cause of the current Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo and has no licensed vaccines or treatments.
 Barbados has become the latest nation to eliminate mother-to-child transmission of HIV as a public health problem, the World Health Organization (WHO) said late last week . Independent certification of the achievement comes after the island nation reported no new HIV infections in infants resulting from mother-to-child transmission from 2022 through 2024. Barbados is one of 26 countries and territories recognized by the WHO for eliminating mother-to-child transmission of HIV, syphilis, or hepatitis B. “This achievement means that children are born free of HIV and that women living with HIV can access the care and treatment they need. It is a proud moment for Barbados, the Caribbean, and the global effort to end AIDS in children,” Jarbas Barbosa, PhD, MPH, Director of the Pan American Health Organization and WHO Regional Director for the Americas, said in a news release.
